# Garoono

> Garoono is the site of Gautam Singh Rathor, a senior software engineer in Delhi who builds mobile apps after his 9 to 5. It lists his apps, sells playbooks and checklists for indie app makers, and has a blog about shipping apps solo next to a day job.

14 apps shipped, 100,000+ users across them, mostly Flutter. Some playbooks are free PDFs, the rest open with a one-time lifetime purchase on the docs page.

# Account Deletion Requirement on the App Store and Google Play

If people can create an account in your app, both stores want them to be able to delete it from inside the app
Apple checks it under guideline 5.1.1(v), Google checks it through its User Data policy and the Data safety form
Deactivating the account does not count on either store
Deleting must remove the account and the data tied to it, and Google also wants a web link that works without the app

That's the whole rule
The rest of this post is how to build it once, properly, and how to prove it to App Review

In October 2026 one of my apps got rejected under 5.1.1(v) for exactly this
It had sign-in and no in-app account deletion
After I added it, Apple asked for a screen recording on a physical device showing the full flow
So this is written from the fix, not from theory

## What Apple requires

Guideline 5.1.1(v) says that if your app supports account creation, you must also offer account deletion within the app ([App Review Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/#data-collection-and-storage))

Apple's account deletion page spells out the details ([Apple](https://developer.apple.com/help/app-review/guideline-reference/5-1-1-account-deletion))

- Make the option easy to find, usually in account settings
- Delete the entire account record and the personal data tied to it
- Only offering to deactivate or disable the account is not enough
- If deletion finishes on your website, link straight to that page, not your home page
- If deletion takes time, tell the user how long and confirm when it's done
- If the law makes you keep some data, say what you keep and what you delete

Two details catch indie devs

Guest accounts count
Apple says people should be able to delete automatically generated accounts and their data too ([Apple](https://developer.apple.com/help/app-review/guideline-reference/5-1-1-account-deletion))

Subscriptions need a warning
If the user has an auto-renewable subscription, Apple wants you to tell them billing continues through Apple and ask them to cancel first ([Apple](https://developer.apple.com/help/app-review/guideline-reference/5-1-1-account-deletion))

You may ask the user to confirm, or enter a code sent to their email
But Apple says apps that make deletion unnecessarily difficult will not pass review, and unless you're in a highly regulated industry, don't make people call, email or chat with support to delete ([Apple](https://developer.apple.com/help/app-review/guideline-reference/5-1-1-account-deletion))

## What Google Play requires

Google's rule is close, with one extra piece

Its User Data policy says apps that allow account creation must offer deletion both inside the app and through a web resource outside it ([Google Play policy](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/10144311))
The same policy says temporary deactivation, disabling or freezing the account does not qualify as deletion

Google's help page on the requirement adds what the web link needs ([Google Play Help](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/13327111))

- It must load without errors
- It must reference your app or developer name as shown on your Play listing
- The user must be able to actually request deletion through it
- You put the link in the Data safety form in Play Console

Why a web link if the app already has a button?
Google's answer is that a user who already uninstalled your app shouldn't have to download it again just to delete their account ([Google Play Help](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/13327111))

You can keep some data for security, fraud prevention or legal reasons, as long as you tell users clearly what you keep ([Google Play Help](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/13327111))

A simple page on your site with a short form, or a page that tells signed in users to tap Delete account and logged out users how to request it, is enough for a small app

## What a deletion flow must actually do

The button is the easy part
What happens after the tap is what makes it real

### 1 Confirm and warn
One screen, one clear button, and a line about active subscriptions with a link to manage them

### 2 Re-authenticate
Firebase says deleting an account is a security-sensitive action that needs a recent sign-in, and fails with an error otherwise ([Firebase docs](https://firebase.google.com/docs/auth/web/manage-users))
So ask the user to sign in again right before deleting, instead of waiting for the error

### 3 Revoke Sign in with Apple
Apple says apps that support Sign in with Apple should use its REST API to revoke user tokens ([Apple](https://developer.apple.com/help/app-review/guideline-reference/5-1-1-account-deletion))
Firebase does not store Apple tokens, so the user signs in with Apple again, you take the fresh authorization code, and Firebase revokes it for you ([Firebase docs](https://firebase.google.com/docs/auth/ios/apple))

### 4 Delete the server data
Firestore documents, Storage files, anything the user posted
Apple says people expect shared content like photos, posts and reviews to go too ([Apple](https://developer.apple.com/help/app-review/guideline-reference/5-1-1-account-deletion))

### 5 Delete the auth user
Last, because your security rules probably check `request.auth` before letting anyone delete those documents

Here's the short Flutter version for an Apple sign-in user

```dart
Future<void> deleteAccount() async {
  final auth = FirebaseAuth.instance;
  final user = auth.currentUser!;

  // Fresh sign-in: satisfies recent-login and gives a new Apple auth code
  final cred = await user.reauthenticateWithProvider(AppleAuthProvider());
  final code = cred.additionalUserInfo?.authorizationCode;
  if (code != null) await auth.revokeTokenWithAuthorizationCode(code);

  // Server data before the auth user, while rules still see request.auth
  await FirebaseFirestore.instance.doc('users/${user.uid}').delete();

  await user.delete();
}
```

The `revokeTokenWithAuthorizationCode` call is straight from the FlutterFire docs ([Firebase docs](https://firebase.google.com/docs/auth/flutter/federated-auth))
For Google or email users, swap the reauthenticate step for that provider and skip the revoke

If a user has subcollections or Storage files, one document delete is not enough
Move the data part into a Cloud Function that deletes everything under the user's ID, and call it from the app

## How to show it to App Review

This is the part Apple came back to me about

Apple's review prep page says to give working demo account credentials in App Store Connect, and to use the Notes field for anything extra reviewers need ([Apple](https://developer.apple.com/help/app-review/before-submitting-for-review/complete-review))
For account deletion, add these to Review Notes before Apple asks

- A demo account that is safe to delete, and a second one in case they delete the first
- The exact path, for example Settings, Account, Delete account
- What gets deleted and how long it takes
- A screen recording on a real iPhone: sign in, find Delete account, finish the deletion

In my case Apple asked for that recording after the rejection
Recording it up front costs five minutes and can save you a full review cycle

> Deleting the account, not hiding it, is the rule on both stores

## Pre-submit checklist

| Check | Pass when |
|---|---|
| In-app button | Delete account is easy to find in account settings |
| Real deletion | Account record and user data are gone, not just flagged |
| Re-auth | Fresh sign-in happens before the delete call |
| Apple token | Revoked for Sign in with Apple users |
| Subscriptions | User is told billing continues and how to cancel |
| Google web link | Loads, names the app, accepts a request, is in Data safety |
| Review Notes | Demo account, path to the button and a device recording |

If you want the other legal checks stores run before approving an app, they're in [Before You Submit: Legal Checklist](/docs/#legal-checklist-before-you-submit)
And my [App Store checklist](/blog/flutter-app-store-checklist/) covers three other blockers that a clean build never catches

## FAQ

### Is account deletion required on the App Store?

Yes, if your app lets people create an account
Guideline 5.1.1(v) requires that those apps also let people delete the account from inside the app

### Is deactivating an account enough?

No
Apple and Google both say that only deactivating, disabling or freezing an account does not count as deletion

### Does Google Play need a web link for account deletion?

Yes
Google wants a working web page where users can request deletion without reinstalling the app, and that link goes in the Data safety form in Play Console

### Do I have to revoke Sign in with Apple tokens when deleting an account?

Apple says apps that support Sign in with Apple should revoke user tokens through its REST API
With Firebase, sign the user in with Apple again and pass the new authorization code to the revoke method before deleting the user

### Can I keep some user data after the account is deleted?

Yes, if the law or fraud prevention requires it
Both stores want you to tell users clearly what you keep

# App Rejected for Guideline 4.3 Spam? What It Means and What to Do

A guideline 4.3 Spam rejection means Apple thinks your app is a duplicate
Either a copy of another app on your own account, or one more variant of something the store already has plenty of
Fixing a bug won't help, because nothing is broken
You get out in one of three ways: merge it into an app you already have, change it until it's clearly different, or answer Apple's questions honestly and show why it isn't spam

I got this one on October 13, 2026
Two of my apps were rejected one minute apart, both under 4.3 Spam plus 4.2.6
One of them overlapped with another app on the same account
Here's what the rules actually say and what I'd do differently

## What guideline 4.3 Spam says

Guideline 4.3 has two parts, and it helps to know which one you hit ([App Review Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/#spam))

### 4.3(a): your own duplicates
Apple's words: "Don't create multiple Bundle IDs of the same app"
The example is a separate map app for every city instead of one map app that searches any city
Apple's suggested fix is right in the rule: submit a single app and provide the variations using in-app purchase

### 4.3(b): the store's duplicates
Apple's words: "Don't submit apps that are indistinguishable from what's already widely available"
It names categories it considers saturated: dating, flashlight, sound effects, wallpaper, simple timers and fortune telling
New apps there are only accepted if they offer "a meaningfully different or improved experience"
And the same paragraph warns that repeated submissions of low-effort apps may lead to removal from the Apple Developer Program

### 4.2.6: template apps
This one sits under Minimum Functionality ([App Review Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/#minimum-functionality))
It says apps "created from a commercialized template or app generation service will be rejected" unless the provider of the app's content submits them
The allowed alternative is one app that hosts every client's content, like a restaurant finder with a page per restaurant

## What my rejection said

Apple's message on my two apps used three phrases that stuck with me

- The app "duplicates functionality" already on the App Store
- It "could be an in-app purchase in another app on your account"
- It "shares code with your other apps"

Read those again and you'll notice none of them are about the app alone
They compare it to my other apps

That's the part most indie devs miss
4.3(a) is about your account, so Apple looks at your app next to everything else you've shipped
Two rejections landing one minute apart told me the reviewer was looking at my catalogue, not at one binary

## Why indie devs get hit

You don't need to be a spammer to look like one

- **Several similar apps**, a viewer for one file type, then another viewer for a similar one, each in its own listing
- **A shared starter kit**, same onboarding, same paywall, same settings screen, same code underneath
- **Template or white label apps**, one codebase, many clients, many bundle IDs, which is exactly what 4.2.6 describes
- **Crowded categories**, a simple timer or wallpaper app built fast with AI lands in a list Apple already called full
- **Copy paste metadata**, same description structure and release notes across apps make the overlap even easier to spot

Reusing code is normal, every solo dev does it
The problem is when the reused code is also the whole product

## What to do after a 4.3 rejection

### Option 1: merge it into an app you already have
If the rejected app does the same job for the same people as one of your other apps, this is the honest answer
Apple's own rule suggests shipping variations as in-app purchases inside a single app
You keep one listing, one set of reviews and one codebase to maintain, which is less work anyway

### Option 2: make substantial changes
If the app really is its own product, make that visible
New core features, a different interface, its own onboarding and screenshots, a description that isn't a copy of your other listings
Renaming the app and swapping colours is not substantial

### Option 3: answer Apple's questions honestly
My rejection came with a list of questions from Apple
Answer every one of them, plainly, with no spin
If the app shares code with your other apps, say so, and explain what is different for the user
Then submit an appeal if you think Apple misread the app

Apple says you can appeal to the App Review Board if you feel they misunderstood your app's concept and functionality ([Apple](https://developer.apple.com/distribute/app-review/))
Its tips: give specific reasons the app complies, submit only one appeal per rejected submission, and answer any requests for information first
You can also book a 30 minute App Review appointment over Webex to ask about guidelines and common rejections ([Apple](https://developer.apple.com/distribute/app-review/))

> Resubmitting the same build unchanged gets the same rejection

That last line isn't just my opinion
One developer on Apple's forums reports two 4.3(a) rejections in a row and then a warning about account removal for repeated noncompliance ([Apple Developer Forums](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/847013))

## Check this before you build the next app

| Question | If yes |
|---|---|
| Does one of my apps already do this job? | Add it as a feature or in-app purchase there |
| Is it a timer, wallpaper, flashlight or similar? | Find a real difference first, or skip it |
| Is it built from a template I sell or reuse for clients? | Ship one app that hosts every client |
| Are screens and paywall copied from my starter kit? | Change the core flow, not just the colours |
| Does the description read like my other listings? | Rewrite it for this app's users |

I now run this table before I start a new app, not after review
It's cheaper to kill an idea at the start than to argue for it later

For the other reasons new apps get rejected and the step by step way to ship, see [Don't Get Rejected: App Store Launch Guide](/docs/#app-store-launch-guide)
My [App Store checklist](/blog/flutter-app-store-checklist/) covers three blockers a clean build never catches, and [the account deletion post](/blog/account-deletion-requirement-app-store/) covers the 5.1.1(v) one

## FAQ

### What does guideline 4.3 Spam mean?

It means Apple thinks your app duplicates another app
Under 4.3(a) that's multiple bundle IDs of the same app on your account, and under 4.3(b) it's an app indistinguishable from what's already widely available on the store

### What is the difference between 4.3(a) and 4.3(b)?

4.3(a) is about your own apps, for example one app per city instead of one app for all cities
4.3(b) is about the whole store, for example another simple flashlight or wallpaper app without a meaningfully different experience

### What is guideline 4.2.6?

It is the rule against apps made from a commercialized template or app generation service
Those apps are rejected unless the provider of the app's content submits them, or all clients live inside one app

### Can I fix a 4.3 rejection by resubmitting?

Not with the same build
Merge the app into one you already have, make substantial changes, or answer Apple's questions honestly and appeal if they misread the app

### Can a 4.3 rejection affect my developer account?

It can if it keeps happening
Apple's guideline says repeated submissions of low-effort apps may lead to removal from the Apple Developer Program

---
Source: https://garoono.in/blog/google-play-12-testers-14-days-requirement/
Date: 2026-10-22

# Google Play 12 Testers 14 Days Requirement: How Solo Devs Pass

If you made a personal Google Play developer account after November 13, 2023, you can't go straight to production
You first run a closed test with at least 12 testers who stay opted in for at least 14 days in a row ([Play Console Help](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/14151465?hl=en))
Then you apply for production access from the Play Console Dashboard and answer questions about that test
Google reviews your answers, and if the test looks thin, it asks you to keep testing

Finding 12 names is the easy part
Keeping 12 real people opted in, and showing they actually used the app, is where solo devs lose weeks
Here's the exact rule, what counts, why access gets refused, and a plan that fits into 1 to 2 hours a night

## Who the rule applies to

The testing requirement covers personal developer accounts created after November 13, 2023 ([Play Console Help](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/6112435?hl=en))
Google's account setup page labels that section "Personal accounts only" ([Play Console Help](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/6112435?hl=en))

So three cases:

| Your account | Closed test needed before production? |
|---|---|
| Personal, created after November 13, 2023 | Yes, 12 testers for 14 days in a row |
| Personal, created on or before November 13, 2023 | No, the rule is for newer accounts |
| Organization | Not covered by the rule as Google writes it |

Organization accounts come with their own paperwork, so don't switch types just to skip testing
I covered which account type fits a solo dev in [Android developer verification for indie developers](/blog/android-developer-verification-for-indie-developers/)

Until you get production access, Production and Pre-registration stay locked in Play Console ([Play Console Help](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/14151465?hl=en))

## The exact rule, in Google's words

Google asks for a closed test with "a minimum of 12 testers who have been opted in continuously for at least 14 days" ([Play Console Help](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/14151465?hl=en))

The word that trips people up is continuously
Google's FAQ says testers who opt in, test for fewer than 14 days and then opt out don't count ([Play Console Help](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/14151465?hl=en))
And if a tester opts out and later opts back in, only a fresh run of 14 consecutive days counts

So 15 testers who drift in and out can still leave you short
12 who join on day one and never leave is a pass on the numbers

## What counts as an opted in tester

Adding an email to a list is not the same as having a tester
Each tester has to open your opt-in link and accept it ([Play Console Help](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9845334?hl=en))

A few details from Google's testing setup page:

- You add testers by email list or by Google Group
- Testers need a Google Account or a Google Workspace account
- With a Google Group, people must join the group before they can opt in
- The opt-in link only shows once the closed track status is Published
- After your first publish, the link can take several hours to work for testers

All of that is on the same [Play Console Help page](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9845334?hl=en)

> A tester only counts after they tap your opt-in link and accept, and only while they stay opted in

My advice: ask each tester to send you a screenshot of the "you're a tester" screen
It takes them ten seconds and it saves you guessing on day 14

## Why production access gets refused

Google names two reasons for asking you to keep testing: fewer than 12 opted in testers, or not enough tester engagement ([Play Console Help](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/14151465?hl=en))

The first is just counting
The second is where the form matters

When you apply, Google asks three groups of questions ([Play Console Help](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/14151465?hl=en)):

- About your closed test: how easy recruiting was, whether testers used all the features, how usage compared to what you expect in production, and a summary of the feedback and how you collected it
- About your app: who it's for, why it's useful, and how many installs you expect in year one
- About production readiness: what you changed because of the test, and how you decided it was ready

Read that list again
Google wants evidence that people used the app and that you acted on what they said
A test where 12 strangers installed once and never opened it again gives you nothing to write

That's why I'm wary of tester swap groups and paid tester packages
They can get you to 12, but they rarely give you feedback worth putting in the form

## A plan that fits after work

### Before day 0, line up 15 to 20 people
Ask more than 12 so one or two dropping out doesn't reset you
Start with people who would use the app anyway: friends, coworkers, family, people who asked you about the idea
If you already have apps live, a short note to those users can find people who like your work
The same channels I use to find [the first 100 app users](/blog/how-to-get-your-first-100-app-users/) work here too

### Day 0, publish the closed track and send the link
Use a Google Group, it's easier to manage than a list of emails
Send one message with the group link, the opt-in link, and what to try first
Collect the opt-in screenshots the same evening

### Days 1 to 14, give testers a reason to open it
Set up a feedback channel, Google suggests email, a website or a messaging group
Ask for one small thing every few days, like trying a single feature
Ship at least one update during the test, Google itself recommends updating your app in closed testing before production
Keep a simple note of every piece of feedback and what you changed

### Day 15, apply with real answers
Count opted in testers in Play Console before you click Apply for production
Fill the form from your notes, name the features people used and the fixes you shipped
Then wait, Google says review usually takes seven days or less ([Play Console Help](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/14151465?hl=en))

## Quick checklist

- [ ] Personal account created after November 13, 2023, so the rule applies
- [ ] 15 to 20 people lined up before you publish the closed track
- [ ] Every tester accepted the opt-in link, with a screenshot to prove it
- [ ] Nobody opted out for 14 days in a row
- [ ] A feedback channel testers actually use
- [ ] At least one update shipped during the test
- [ ] Form answers written from real feedback, not guesses

## Get past it in one go

I wrote down how to get Play production access on the first try, with testers who actually test, in [Stuck at 12 Testers](/docs/#stuck-at-12-testers)

## FAQ

### Does the 12 testers rule apply to organization accounts?

Google's rule covers personal developer accounts created after November 13, 2023
Organization accounts are not covered by it as Google writes it

### What happens if a tester opts out before 14 days?

That tester stops counting toward the requirement
If they opt back in, they need a new run of 14 consecutive days to count

### Do testers have to install the app or just join the list?

Each tester has to accept your opt-in link, being on the email list or Google Group is not enough
Google also checks engagement, so testers should install the app and use it

### Can I use paid testers or tester exchange groups?

They can get you to 12 opted in testers
Google asks about tester engagement and feedback when you apply, so testers who never use the app make it harder to get access

### How long does the production access review take?

Google says review usually takes seven days or less, and occasionally longer
If Google asks you to keep testing, run the closed test longer and apply again

Source: https://garoono.in/blog/privacy-policy-for-app-store-submission/
Date: 2026-10-22

# Privacy Policy for App Store Submission: Apple and Google Rules

Every app needs a privacy policy to get through review on the App Store and Google Play, even one that collects nothing
Both stores want the link in two places: a field in the developer console, and inside the app itself
Then each has its own data form, App Privacy details on Apple and the Data safety form on Google, and the policy has to agree with it
If your app has accounts, both stores also want account deletion, and Google wants a web link for it

The rest is the detail, so your policy passes on the first round

## What Apple checks

### The rule
Guideline 5.1.1(i) says all apps must include a privacy policy link "in the App Store Connect metadata field and within the app in an easily accessible manner" ([App Review Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/#data-collection-and-storage))

The same guideline lists what the policy must say ([App Review Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/#data-collection-and-storage)):

- What data the app collects, how it collects it, and every use of it
- That any third party you share data with, like analytics tools, ad networks and SDKs, gives the same protection your policy promises
- How long you keep data, how you delete it, and how a user can revoke consent or ask for deletion

Free templates often skip that last point, so check yours

### Where the URL goes
In App Store Connect, open your app, pick App privacy in the sidebar, and click Edit next to Privacy Policy ([App Store Connect Help](https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-app-information/manage-app-privacy))
Apple says a privacy policy URL is required for all apps, and the user privacy choices URL next to it is optional ([App Store Connect Help](https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-app-information/manage-app-privacy))
One catch: a change to these URLs goes live with your next app version

### App Privacy details
This is the privacy label on your product page
Apple says it's required to submit new apps and app updates, and it must include the practices of third-party partners whose code is in your app ([Apple](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/app-privacy-details/))

Apple defines collect as sending data off the device in a way that lets you or your partners access it for longer than it takes to handle the request in real time ([Apple](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/app-privacy-details/))
So the Firebase, crash reporting or ads SDK you added in ten minutes counts, even if you never look at that data

You can update these answers any time without shipping a new build ([Apple](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/app-privacy-details/))
And guideline 2.3 asks that your metadata, privacy information included, matches what the app really does ([App Review Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/#accurate-metadata))

AI features add one more step on Apple, see [my App Store checklist](/blog/flutter-app-store-checklist/)

## What Google checks

### The rule
Google's User Data policy says all apps must post a privacy policy link in the designated field in Play Console, and a link or the text inside the app ([Play Console Help](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/10144311?hl=en))
Apps that don't access any personal or sensitive data still need one ([Play Console Help](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/10144311?hl=en))

Google's list of what the policy must cover ([Play Console Help](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/10144311?hl=en)):

- Who you are, and a way to contact you about privacy
- The types of personal and sensitive data the app accesses, collects, uses and shares, and who it's shared with
- How you handle that data securely
- How long you keep data and how you delete it
- A clear label, like a title that says privacy policy

### The URL rules
Google wants the policy on an active, public, non-geofenced URL, not a PDF, and not editable by visitors ([Play Console Help](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/10144311?hl=en))
The developer name on your Play listing has to appear in the policy, or the app has to be named in it ([Play Console Help](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/10144311?hl=en))

### The Data safety form
Every app published on Google Play needs a Data safety form, even if it collects no user data ([Play Console Help](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/10787469?hl=en))
It has to include data handled by third-party libraries and SDKs in your app ([Play Console Help](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/10787469?hl=en))

Google says you alone are responsible for complete and accurate declarations, and apps that don't comply face enforcement ([Play Console Help](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/10787469?hl=en))

## If your app has accounts

Apple says apps that support account creation must let people start account deletion inside the app ([Apple](https://developer.apple.com/support/offering-account-deletion-in-your-app/))
Only offering to deactivate or disable the account is not enough, and the option should be easy to find, usually in account settings ([Apple](https://developer.apple.com/support/offering-account-deletion-in-your-app/))
With Sign in with Apple, Apple also asks you to revoke the user's tokens through its REST API

Google wants the same in-app option, plus a way to request deletion outside the app, like a page on your website ([Play Console Help](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/10144311?hl=en))
That web link goes into the Data safety form in Play Console ([Play Console Help](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/13327111?hl=en))

Google's rules for that page ([Play Console Help](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/13327111?hl=en)):

- It loads without errors
- It names the app or developer as shown on your Play listing
- The deletion steps are easy to find on the page
- Users can request deletion without reinstalling the app
- It says what data you keep, if any, and why

Freezing or deactivating the account doesn't count as deletion, and you must delete the user data tied to the account too ([Play Console Help](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/10144311?hl=en))

> Your privacy policy, your data form and your app have to tell the same story, a policy that's fine on its own still fails if the form says something else

## Where solo devs slip

None of these are hard, just easy to forget at 1am

- The policy came from a generator and never mentions the SDKs you added later
- The data forms say "no data collected" while Firebase Analytics or an ads SDK runs in the background
- The policy is a PDF or a doc link, which Google rules out
- The policy names a different developer than your store listing
- The in-app link is buried three screens deep, or missing from the logged out state

If your policy promises secure data handling, make it true first with [the RLS checklist](/blog/supabase-rls-checklist-for-vibe-coded-apps/)

## The checklist

| Check | Apple | Google |
|---|---|---|
| Public policy URL in the console | App privacy page in App Store Connect | Privacy policy field in Play Console |
| Link inside the app | Easy to reach | Link or text in the app |
| Says what you collect and why | Required | Required |
| Covers third-party SDKs | Required | Required |
| Retention and deletion explained | Required | Required |
| Contact details and policy title | Good practice | Required |
| Format | Public web page | Public web page, no PDF, not geofenced |
| Data form filled and matches | App Privacy details | Data safety form |
| Account deletion, if you have accounts | In the app | In the app, plus a web URL in Data safety |

Run it once per app, then again any time you add an SDK

## The full legal pass

The privacy policy is one of seven things stores check before approving an app, all seven are in [Before You Submit: Legal Checklist](/docs/#legal-checklist-before-you-submit)

## FAQ

### Do I need a privacy policy if my app collects no data?

Yes, Apple requires a privacy policy link for all apps
Google says apps that do not access any personal or sensitive user data must still submit a privacy policy

### Where do I add the privacy policy URL in App Store Connect?

Open your app in App Store Connect, select App privacy in the sidebar, and click Edit next to Privacy Policy
Changes to the URL go live with your next app version

### Can my privacy policy be a PDF or a Google Doc?

Not for Google Play, the policy must be on an active, public, non-geofenced URL, no PDFs, and not editable
A plain page on your own website works for both stores

### Does the privacy policy have to mention third-party SDKs?

Yes, Apple asks you to confirm that third parties like analytics tools, ad networks and SDKs give user data the same protection
Apple's App Privacy details and Google's Data safety form must also include data collected by SDKs in your app

### Do I need an account deletion link for Google Play?

Only if your app lets users create an account
Then you need a delete option inside the app and a web link for deletion requests, entered in the Data safety form

Date: 2026-10-14

# Apple Blocked My Flutter Apps 3 Times: My App Store Checklist

All three builds compiled, signed and uploaded without a single warning
Then App Review stopped them anyway

I'm a solo dev with about 16 Flutter apps live on iOS and Android
This year two of them, PushPass and GetUp, ran into three different App Store blockers
No crashes, no bugs Flutter could have caught
Just policy, metadata and one entitlement Xcode never complained about

Apple says over 40% of unresolved issues relate to guideline 2.1, App Completeness ([Apple](https://developer.apple.com/distribute/app-review/))
That matches my year, so here's what each blocker looked like, and the checklist that now runs before every iOS release

## The 30 second version

If your app sends user data to any AI model, answer "who, what, where" in App Review Notes and ask for consent in the app before the first upload

If you sell auto-renewable subscriptions, every App Store description in every locale ends with a Terms of Use (EULA) link

If you use Screen Time APIs, request the Family Controls Distribution entitlement for the app and every extension on the day you add the feature

## Blocker 1: Information Needed on an AI feature

GetUp 1.1.2, October 2026
Not a hard rejection, a Guideline 2.1 "Information Needed" message

Apple asked three things:

- Who hosts the AI model?
- Is it third-party AI?
- Does user data go to it?

It lines up with a rule Apple changed on November 13, 2025 ([Apple](https://developer.apple.com/news/?id=ey6d8onl))
Guideline 5.1.2(i) now says you must disclose where personal data is shared with third parties, "including with third-party AI, and obtain explicit permission before doing so" ([App Review Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/#data-use-and-sharing))

That sentence has two jobs in it
Disclosure, and permission

Here's what I now put in App Review Notes for any app that touches a model, before Apple has to ask:

- Which parts run on device and which run in the cloud
- The provider's name, for example Google's Gemini through Firebase AI Logic
- Exactly what data is sent, field by field
- How long the provider keeps it and whether it's used for training
- Where the consent screen is and how a reviewer reaches it

Then the in-app part
The AI provider goes into the third-party list in your privacy policy, by name
And the user agrees before the first upload, on a screen that says what goes where

> A Settings toggle that's on by default is not consent

One more lesson from that review
When you reply to an Information Needed message, describe the build Apple actually reviewed, not the one on your laptop
If that build has no consent screen, don't promise one in your reply
Remove it from review, ship the fixed build, and put the answer in its Review Notes

Here's a minimal consent gate with `flutter_bloc`, default is false, always

```dart
class AiConsentCubit extends Cubit<bool> {
  AiConsentCubit(this._prefs) : super(_prefs.getBool(_key) ?? false);
  static const _key = 'ai_consent_v1';
  final SharedPreferences _prefs;

  Future<void> grant() async {
    await _prefs.setBool(_key, true);
    emit(true);
  }
}

Future<void> analyzePhoto(BuildContext context, Uint8List photo) async {
  final consent = context.read<AiConsentCubit>();
  final ai = context.read<AiRepository>();
  if (!consent.state) {
    final agreed = await showAiConsentSheet(context);
    if (agreed != true) return;
    await consent.grant();
  }
  await ai.analyze(photo);
}
```

Every call to the model goes through that one function
If someone adds a second path that skips it, code review catches it because it's the only place `AiRepository` gets called

## Blocker 2: The EULA link nobody puts in the description

This one is boring and it still blocked a submission

If your app has auto-renewable subscriptions, Apple says your app and your App Store metadata must include links to your Terms of Use and Privacy Policy ([Apple](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/subscriptions/))

Privacy has its own field in App Store Connect
Terms of Use, if you use Apple's standard EULA, doesn't
So it goes at the end of the App Store description

Miss it and automated review blocks the submission before a human ever looks

The trap is the words "every locale"
Localize into eight languages and you have eight descriptions
Someone rewrites the German one for a keyword push and drops the footer, and that's enough

So don't paste it by hand
Bake the link into your listing source, and let a tiny script check every locale before upload
If you keep metadata in fastlane, it's this:

```dart
import 'dart:io';

const eula =
    'https://www.apple.com/legal/internet-services/itunes/dev/stdeula/';

void main() {
  final missing = Directory('fastlane/metadata')
      .listSync()
      .whereType<Directory>()
      .map((d) => File('${d.path}/description.txt'))
      .where((f) => f.existsSync() && !f.readAsStringSync().contains(eula))
      .map((f) => f.parent.path)
      .toList();
  if (missing.isNotEmpty) {
    stderr.writeln('EULA link missing in: ${missing.join(', ')}');
    exit(1);
  }
  stdout.writeln('EULA link found in every locale');
}
```

That's the standard Apple EULA URL
If you wrote your own terms, check for your URL instead

And don't forget the paywall
The same Apple page lists what the sign-up screen itself must show: the subscription name and length, the full renewal price, and a way to restore purchases ([Apple](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/subscriptions/))
Put the two links there too

## Blocker 3: Family Controls, the entitlement that sails through TestFlight

This is the nasty one, it hit both PushPass and GetUp

If your app uses Screen Time APIs (FamilyControls, ManagedSettings, DeviceActivity, shield extensions), you need the Family Controls entitlement
There's a Development version and a Distribution version

The Development capability builds, it signs, it uploads, and TestFlight is happy
Then App Review blocks it

Apple's Family Controls setup guide covers the part people miss: the Screen Time extensions, like Device Activity Monitor, Device Activity Report, Shield Action and Shield Configuration, need the capability on their own App IDs too ([Apple](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/xcode/configuring-family-controls))
A blocker app can easily have four bundle IDs, which can mean four requests through the [distribution request form](https://developer.apple.com/contact/request/family-controls-distribution)

Flutter makes this easy to miss
Those extensions live in the `ios` folder as native targets
`flutter build ipa` builds them, signs them, and never says a word about distribution

And approvals are not fast
Developers on Apple's forums report requests sitting in "Submitted" for weeks ([Apple Developer Forums](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/824193))

One update worth knowing
In a 2026 forum reply, Apple said approval can now be scoped to the whole team instead of each bundle ID ([Apple Developer Forums](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/828085))
That wasn't how mine went, so don't assume either way
Open Certificates, Identifiers & Profiles and check that every single identifier shows Family Controls as assigned for distribution

My rule now: request it the same day the Screen Time feature gets added, not the day before submitting

## The checklist I run before every iOS submit

| Check | Pass when |
|---|---|
| AI calls | Review Notes answer is written and the provider is in the privacy policy |
| AI consent | Fresh install shows consent before the first upload, and "no" means no upload |
| Toggles | No consent toggle defaults to on |
| EULA script | Every locale ends with the Terms of Use link and the privacy link |
| Paywall | Plan name, length, full price, restore and both links are visible |
| Screen Time | Every bundle ID, app and each extension, shows Family Controls Distribution |
| Login | Demo account details are in Review Notes |
| Replies | An Information Needed answer describes the build under review, not the next one |

Eight lines, much cheaper than another round of review

## Quick answers

### Does on-device AI count as third-party AI?

The rule is about sharing personal data with third parties
Data that never leaves the phone isn't shared
But say in Review Notes which parts run on device and which don't, it answers the question before it's asked

### Can I just use Apple's standard EULA?

Yes, link the standard EULA URL in the description
If you wrote custom terms, you can add them in App Store Connect instead

### Is Family Controls approval per app or per team?

Apple's setup guide puts the capability on each extension, and a newer forum reply talks about team-wide approval
Check the portal for every identifier before you submit

### Will TestFlight catch any of this?

No
TestFlight tests your binary
These were about metadata, consent and entitlements, and the Family Controls build installs and runs fine from TestFlight

## My takeaway

None of these were hard
Each one was a single line, a single link or a single form

What made them expensive was finding out at review time
So the checklist runs before the upload, every time, for every app

I put the full 30 minute pre-submit audit, with every check that gets small apps rejected, into one doc

Source: https://garoono.in/blog/flutter-apps-revenue-honest-numbers/
Date: 2026-10-13

# 100,000 Downloads, $216 a Month: My Flutter Apps Revenue

I have about 16 Flutter apps live on iOS and Android
Together they've been installed around 100,000 times

They make about $216 a month in recurring revenue
Not per app, in total

Most indie income posts show the chart that went up and to the right
This is the other kind
I pulled my RevenueCat, PostHog and AdMob numbers on October 12, 2026
They're rounded and approximate, but they're real

## The 30 second version

100,000 installs sounds like a business, it isn't one yet
One app makes most of the money, iOS users pay about 12 times more than Android users, and my full-screen ads barely show
So I'm going iOS first, aiming at richer markets, fixing one paywall and freezing the apps that don't earn

## The numbers, no filter

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Apps live | About 16, all Flutter, most on Firebase |
| Lifetime installs | About 100,000 |
| Revenue, last 28 days | About $256 |
| MRR | About $216 from 104 active subscriptions |
| XLSheetAI share of MRR | About $140, roughly two thirds |
| Revenue per 1,000 new iOS users | About $234 |
| Revenue per 1,000 new Android users | About $19 |
| India | Almost two thirds of new users, under a third of revenue |
| AdMob, last month | About $3.40 across every app |

## What worked

### One app found a real job to do

XLSheetAI is an AI helper for spreadsheets
People open it when they're stuck on a formula at work
That's a problem with money attached, and it's the only app in my portfolio that earns something every month

### Retention can be built

JapMala, a prayer bead counter, keeps about 1 in 3 users on day one and about 1 in 5 into week two
That's my best retention by far

It earns almost nothing
But it proved I can make an app people come back to on their own

### Flutter was never the problem

One codebase let me ship 16 apps on two stores as a solo dev
No regrets there
Every problem below is a business problem, not a tech one

## What didn't work

### Counting installs instead of buyers

I chased downloads for years
Most of mine came from Android and from India
Those users are real, and I like building for them
But in my apps, one new iOS user is worth about 12 new Android users

It's not just me
RevenueCat's State of Subscription Apps 2026 puts median 14 day revenue per install at $0.38 in North America and $0.08 in India and Southeast Asia ([RevenueCat](https://www.revenuecat.com/state-of-subscription-apps))

### Shipping wide instead of deep

16 apps means 16 paywalls, 16 store listings and 16 sets of reviews to answer
Most of mine got one launch and then nothing
Eight of them make close to zero

### Trusting ads to fill the gap

I added interstitial and rewarded ads to pay for free users
They loaded fine, then they were shown about once in every 50 loads

So almost all my ad money came from small banners
And most of my ad traffic came from India, where my eCPM was about $0.16
In the US it was about $12.39

> Ads don't pay when they don't show, and when they do show, they pay by where your users live

### A paywall that loses buyers at the very last step

In XLSheetAI, 1,109 people saw the paywall in 30 days
275 tapped buy
About 26 finished

Roughly 5 out of every 6 of those purchase starts were cancelled on Apple's or Google's own payment sheet
These people wanted it enough to tap the button
Then something on that last screen changed their mind
I'm writing that funnel up in detail next

### Flying blind for a while

In PushPass, the PostHog key came from `--dart-define` only
From `v1.2.2` on, builds went out without it, `String.fromEnvironment` returned an empty string, and the SDK quietly switched itself off
Every analytics event after that was lost

Now release builds fall back to a bundled `.env` and shout when a key is missing:

```dart
import 'package:flutter/foundation.dart';
import 'package:flutter_dotenv/flutter_dotenv.dart';

const _fromDefine = String.fromEnvironment('POSTHOG_KEY');

String posthogKey() {
  final key = _fromDefine.isNotEmpty
      ? _fromDefine
      : (dotenv.env['POSTHOG_KEY'] ?? '');
  if (key.isEmpty) debugPrint('POSTHOG_KEY MISSING: analytics is OFF');
  return key;
}
```

If you take one thing from this post, take that
You can't fix a funnel you can't see

## What I'm changing next

- **iOS first**, new features and new apps ship on iOS first, and Android follows once the iOS version earns
- **Tier 1 markets**, listings, screenshots and tests aimed at the US, UK and Europe, instead of wherever installs happen to come from
- **Fix the one paywall that matters**, XLSheetAI gets a free trial on the yearly plan, a clearer price on the paywall itself and a cheaper intro offer, before I touch any other app
- **Freeze the tail**, Fitess, Forma, Repvolve, JSON View, NailMirror, Focuson, SparkMate and Habitide stay live, but get bug fixes only

Number 4 is the hard one
Each of those apps was a weekend I was proud of
But 16 half-loved apps lost to one app that people actually need

## Quick answers

### Should Flutter devs skip Android?

No
Android still brought most of my users and some of my revenue
One codebase means it costs almost nothing extra
I just stop building for it first

### Are ads worth it in a small Flutter app?

Only if full-screen ads actually show, and only if your users live in markets that pay
Check the show rate in AdMob, not just the match rate

### Why freeze apps instead of deleting them?

Live apps still pick up a few installs and cost me almost nothing to keep
Freezing stops the time drain without throwing anything away

### What would you do differently from day one?

Put events on the paywall before launch: paywall view, purchase start, purchase cancelled, purchase success
Launch on iOS
Build one app deep before starting a second

## The takeaway

100,000 downloads didn't make me a business
One app with a real job, users in markets that pay and a paywall that doesn't scare people at the last step might

Next goal: $500 MRR, mostly from iOS
I'll post the honest numbers again when I get there, or when I don't

The events I track in week one, and the ones I ignore, are all in one doc

Source: https://garoono.in/blog/android-developer-verification-for-indie-developers/
Date: 2026-09-30

# Android Developer Verification for Indie Developers: 2026 Guide

From today, some Android phones will refuse to install apps from developers Google has not verified
Next year that goes global, India included
If you only publish on Google Play, you are probably fine, but "probably" is not a plan

Here is what changed, what you actually need to do, and the one mistake that can lock you out of your own app

## What changed on September 30, 2026

Google now requires apps to be registered by verified developers before they can be installed or updated on certified Android devices in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand ([Android Developers Blog](https://android-developers.googleblog.com/2026/03/android-developer-verification-rolling-out-to-all-developers.html))
Google says it will roll the requirement out globally from 2027 ([Android Developers Blog](https://android-developers.googleblog.com/2026/03/android-developer-verification-rolling-out-to-all-developers.html))

For now it covers installs from the participating stores, Google Play among them
Apps sideloaded directly or shipped through other stores are not affected yet, but Google recommends verifying before the global rollout ([Android developer verification FAQ](https://developer.android.com/developer-verification/guides/faq))

## Do you need to do anything?

### If you publish only on Google Play
Google says that if you have completed Play Console's developer verification, your identity is already verified and eligible Play apps are registered for you automatically ([Android Developers Blog](https://android-developers.googleblog.com/2026/03/android-developer-verification-rolling-out-to-all-developers.html))
Open Play Console, confirm your account verification is complete, and check that each app shows as registered
That is a two minute job, do it today

### If you use Play App Signing
Good news, Google says apps using Play App Signing are part of the automatic registration ([Android developer verification FAQ](https://developer.android.com/developer-verification/guides/faq))

### If you share APKs outside Play
This is where indie devs get caught
Direct APK downloads from your website, betas shared on Telegram, or builds on other stores all need a verified developer once the global rollout reaches your users

> The mistake that locks you out: Google says if you lose your signing key, you won't be able to register your packages ([Android developer verification FAQ](https://developer.android.com/developer-verification/guides/faq))

Back up your signing and upload keys somewhere safe tonight
If an old app was never enrolled in Play App Signing, check where its key lives before 2027

## Which account type do you need?

| Your situation | What to use | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Apps only on Google Play | Your existing Play Console account | Nothing new |
| APKs on your site or other stores | Full distribution Android Developer Console account | $25 fee |
| Apps for family, friends or a small group | Limited distribution account, up to 20 devices, no government ID | Free |
| Publishing as a company | Organisation account with a D-U-N-S number | Takes up to 28 days |

Sources for the table: the $25 fee, the 20 device limit and the D-U-N-S timing all come from Google's help centre ([Android Developer Console Help](https://support.google.com/android-developer-console/answer/16561738?hl=en))
If you plan to register as a company, start the D-U-N-S request now, not in December 2026

## What developers in India should do now

India is not in the first four countries, so nothing changes for your users this year
It is part of the 2027 global rollout, so use the quiet months to get ready

For individual developers in India, Google Play accepts an Indian passport, driving licence, voter ID or PAN card as photo ID ([Google Play Help](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/15633622?hl=en&co=GENIE.CountryCode%3DIN))
Your proof of address has to show your name and address exactly as they appear on your developer profile ([Google Play Help](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/15633622?hl=en&co=GENIE.CountryCode%3DIN))
A mismatch between the name on your PAN and your profile name is an easy way to get stuck, so fix that first

## Can I still test and sideload?

Yes, for development
Google says developers are free to install apps without verification using ADB ([Android developer verification FAQ](https://developer.android.com/developer-verification/guides/faq))
For a handful of real testers outside Play, the free limited distribution account covers up to 20 devices ([Android Developer Console Help](https://support.google.com/android-developer-console/answer/16561738?hl=en))

## Why so many developers are angry

Google frames this as anti malware, citing an analysis of apps from internet sideloaded sources
F-Droid says it has not seen that analysis and calls developer verification an existential threat to free software distribution platforms like F-Droid and to emerging Play Store competitors ([F-Droid](https://f-droid.org/en/2025/10/28/sideloading.html))

My take as someone shipping on Play: for Play only indies this is mostly paperwork
The real cost lands on people who distribute outside Play, and on anyone who lost a signing key years ago

## Your checklist before 2027

- Confirm Play Console developer verification is complete
- Check every app shows as registered
- Back up signing and upload keys in two places
- Enroll old apps in Play App Signing where possible
- Match your profile name and address to your ID and address proof
- Decide your account type if you ship APKs outside Play
- Start a D-U-N-S request early if you publish as a company

## Ship without surprises

Verification is one more box between you and a live app
I keep a full launch guide with the store rules that trip up solo developers most in the docs

Source: https://garoono.in/blog/how-to-get-your-first-100-app-users/
Date: 2026-09-30

# How to Get Your First 100 App Users Without Ads

Your first 100 users are not a marketing problem
They are a finding problem
Somewhere there are 100 people who already feel the pain your app solves
Your job is to stand where they already look, not to shout louder than everyone else

I have shipped 14 apps next to a full time job and crossed 100K users across them
None of that started with an ad budget
This is the playbook I run for every launch now

## Why the first 100 are a different game

The first 100 users are not about scale
They are about proof
Proof that a stranger will install it, understand it and come back tomorrow

That changes what you should spend time on
Forget growth hacks built for apps with a million users
Pick channels where a solo builder can win with effort instead of money

> Rule of thumb: if a channel needs a budget to start, it is not a first 100 channel

## Start where people already search

Most people find apps by typing a problem into the store search bar
Apple says almost 65% of App Store downloads happen directly after a search ([Apple Ads](https://ads.apple.com/app-store/))
It also says 70% of App Store visitors use search to discover apps ([Apple Ads](https://ads.apple.com/app-store/))

So before you post anywhere, fix the listing
Put the main problem in the title and subtitle, in the words users actually use
Read the 1 and 2 star reviews of the top 10 competing apps and steal their vocabulary
Make the first two screenshots explain the outcome, not the features

A listing that ranks for one long tail search can bring a trickle of users every single day
That trickle is how most of my apps got their first users while I slept

## Pick 2 channels, not 15

The mistake I see most is trying every channel for one day each
Nothing works in one day
Pick two channels and give each of them two focused weeks

Here is how I think about the options when I have 1 to 2 hours a night

## The 5 channels that work at zero budget

### 1 Your store listing
Covered above, and it keeps working after you stop
Revisit it every two weeks with what new users tell you

### 2 Twenty direct messages
Find 20 people who publicly complained about the exact problem
Search X, Reddit and niche forums for the complaint in plain words
Send each one a short, honest note with the link and ask for blunt feedback
Most will ignore you
The few who reply become your first loyal users and your best source of copy

### 3 Reddit, done right
Reddit hates promotion and loves useful people
Answer questions in your niche for a week before you ever mention the app
When you do share it, share the story of why you built it and what you learned
Read every rule of the subreddit first, some ban self promotion completely

### 4 Building in public
Post what you shipped, what broke and the real numbers
It is slow at the start because you have no audience
It compounds, and it turns every future launch into a warm launch

### 5 Your other apps
If you have shipped before, your old users are the cheapest channel you own
A small card inside an existing app can send more installs than a week of posting
This is why I keep every app I ship alive, even the small ones

## A 14 day plan you can run after work

| Days | Focus | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| 1 to 3 | Fix the store listing | Title, subtitle and first two screenshots rewritten |
| 4 to 7 | 20 direct messages | 20 sent, every reply logged |
| 8 to 12 | One community | 5 genuinely useful answers, then one story post |
| 13 to 14 | Review | You know which channel gets the next two weeks |

Keep a simple sheet with the source of every install you can trace
After 14 days the pattern is usually obvious

## What not to do

Do not buy installs
They inflate the numbers and teach you nothing about real users
Do not launch on ten directories on the same day and call it marketing
Do not wait for the app to feel finished, it never will

## Keep the loop short

Ship, ask, fix, repeat
Your first 100 users will tell you what the next 1,000 need
Listen to them more than to any growth thread

If you want the full list, I put every zero budget channel I have tested into one free doc, ranked by effort and return

Source: https://garoono.in/blog/supabase-rls-checklist-for-vibe-coded-apps/
Date: 2026-09-30

# Supabase RLS Checklist for Vibe Coded Apps After 16,326 Leaks

Your AI agent built the app in a weekend
It also may have left your users table open to anyone with a browser
This is not a scare story, it is a fresh study, and the fix takes about an hour

This post is the checklist I would run on any Supabase backed app before shipping it
It works whether you wrote the code or Claude, Cursor or Lovable did

## What the research found

On September 25, 2026, UpGuard published a study of roughly 300,000 domains that use Supabase ([UpGuard](https://www.upguard.com/blog/everything-everywhere-systemic-data-exposure-in-supabase-apps))
It found 16,326 databases exposing readable tables to anyone ([UpGuard](https://www.upguard.com/blog/everything-everywhere-systemic-data-exposure-in-supabase-apps))
Over half of those databases had indicators of personal data ([UpGuard](https://www.upguard.com/blog/everything-everywhere-systemic-data-exposure-in-supabase-apps))

Indie makers are not immune
A January 2026 scan of 20,052 products listed on indie launch directories found 11.04% of domains exposing Supabase credentials ([SupaExplorer report](https://supaexplorer.com/cybersecurity-insight-report-january-2026))
TrustMRR listings had the highest rate at 23.76% ([SupaExplorer report](https://supaexplorer.com/cybersecurity-insight-report-january-2026))

> The pattern is almost always the same: a table without Row Level Security, reached with a key that was meant to be public

## Why vibe coded apps leak

Supabase turns on Row Level Security by default for tables you create in its Table Editor
UpGuard points out the gap: tables created programmatically through the API, which is how coding agents talk to Supabase, do not get RLS by default ([UpGuard](https://www.upguard.com/blog/everything-everywhere-systemic-data-exposure-in-supabase-apps))

So the agent creates `profiles`, `orders` and `messages`, the app works, and every row is readable
Nothing looks broken, which is exactly why nobody notices

## Is the Supabase anon key safe in my app?

Yes, if RLS is on
Supabase says the publishable key is safe to expose in a web page, a mobile app or source code, and that it only reaches what Row Level Security allows ([Supabase docs](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/api/api-keys))

The secret key is a different animal
Supabase says a secret key bypasses every Row Level Security policy you have, and to never put one in a browser, a shipped application or source control ([Supabase docs](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/api/api-keys))
If your AI agent pasted a secret or `service_role` key into client code, treat it as leaked and rotate it

## The October 30, 2026 change you should know about

Until now, new tables in the `public` schema were automatically exposed to the `anon`, `authenticated` and `service_role` roles ([Supabase changelog](https://supabase.com/changelog/45329-breaking-change-tables-not-exposed-to-data-and-graphql-api-automatically))
From October 30, 2026, existing projects stop getting those automatic grants, and new tables need explicit grants to be reachable through the API ([Supabase changelog](https://supabase.com/changelog/45329-breaking-change-tables-not-exposed-to-data-and-graphql-api-automatically))

This is good for security, but it can break an app that silently relied on the old behaviour
Add grants on purpose, table by table, and only the ones each role needs

## The 9 step checklist

### 1 Find every table without RLS
Run this in the Supabase SQL editor

```sql
select tablename, rowsecurity
from pg_tables
where schemaname = 'public'
order by rowsecurity, tablename;
```

Any row with `rowsecurity = false` is open to whatever the grants allow

### 2 Turn RLS on for all of them

```sql
alter table public.profiles enable row level security;
```

With RLS on and no policies, the API returns nothing, which is the safe starting point

### 3 Write the narrowest policy that works
The most common one: a signed in user can read only their own rows

```sql
create policy "Users read own rows"
on public.profiles for select
to authenticated
using ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);
```

### 4 Add separate policies for insert, update and delete
Use `with check` so a user cannot write rows that belong to someone else
Skip any operation your app does not need

### 5 Grant access on purpose
Give `anon` only what logged out users truly need, often nothing
Give `authenticated` only the operations your policies cover

### 6 Test like an attacker
Call the REST endpoint for each table with only the publishable key and no user session

```bash
curl "https://YOUR_PROJECT.supabase.co/rest/v1/profiles?select=*" \
  -H "apikey: YOUR_PUBLISHABLE_KEY"
```

You want an empty list or an error, never real rows

### 7 Keep secret keys on the server
Secret keys belong in Edge Functions or your own server, never in a Flutter build, a React bundle or a public repo
Anything shipped inside an app can be extracted

### 8 Move AI provider keys behind a function
The same rule applies to OpenAI or Gemini keys in AI wrapper apps
Even Firebase, whose normal API keys are fine to ship, says a Gemini Developer API key should never be included in your code or configuration files ([Firebase docs](https://firebase.google.com/docs/projects/api-keys))

### 9 Tell your agent the rules up front
Paste this into your project rules file so every new table starts locked

> Every table you create in Supabase must have Row Level Security enabled in the same migration
> Add an explicit policy for each operation the app uses, and explicit grants per role
> Never use or print the service role key in client code

## Quick reference

| Check | Pass when |
|---|---|
| RLS on every public table | The SQL above shows no `false` rows |
| Policies per operation | Select, insert, update and delete each have a policy or are not granted |
| Anon test | Publishable key alone returns no real data |
| Secret key | Only in server code, rotated if it was ever shipped |
| AI keys | Called from a server function, not the app |
| Grants after Oct 30 | Added on purpose for each table and role |

## Using Firebase instead?

The idea is the same with different names
Firebase says its API keys do not need to be treated as secrets, and that data security is enforced by Firebase Security Rules, not by hiding the key ([Firebase docs](https://firebase.google.com/docs/projects/api-keys))
So the Firebase version of this checklist is: no test mode rules in production, rules that check `request.auth` on every collection, and App Check for extra protection

## Before you ship

Run steps 1 and 6 tonight, they take ten minutes and catch most leaks
Then work through the rest before your next release

I put the 8 holes AI most often leaves in Flutter and Firebase apps into one doc, with the fix for each
